questions.q: What does the Weak Law of Large Numbers guarantee about the sample mean X̄ₙ as n grows?
options: X̄ₙ is always exactly equal to the true mean μ
The probability that X̄ₙ deviates from μ by more than any fixed amount goes to zero
The variance of the data itself shrinks to zero
questions.explain: The Weak LLN states P(|X̄ₙ − μ| > ε) → 0 for any ε > 0 — the sample mean converges to the true mean in probability. It says nothing about the shape of the distribution; that's the CLT's job.

questions.q: What is the key condition required for the Central Limit Theorem to apply to i.i.d. random variables?
options: The individual random variables must already be normally distributed
The individual random variables must have finite mean and finite variance
The sample size must be infinite
The individual random variables must be symmetric
questions.explain: The CLT requires only finite mean and finite variance — the shape of the underlying distribution (skewed, bounded, discrete, etc.) does not matter. It fails for distributions with infinite variance.

questions.q: A return series has standard deviation σ = 0.02. What is the standard error of the sample mean using n = 400 observations?
You quadruple your sample size from n to 4n. By what factor does the standard error of the mean shrink?
options: It shrinks by a factor of 4
It shrinks by a factor of 2
It shrinks by a factor of 16
questions.explain: Standard error scales as 1/√n, so quadrupling n (√4 = 2) halves the standard error — not a fourfold reduction.

questions.q: Why can the classical Central Limit Theorem fail for certain heavy-tailed financial return series?
options: Because the mean of the data is negative
Because the data has infinite or undefined variance, violating the theorem's key assumption
Because the data is measured daily rather than monthly
Because the sample size is always too small in finance
questions.explain: The classical CLT requires finite variance. Some heavy-tailed distributions have infinite variance, and averages of such variables converge instead to a different (stable) family, not the normal distribution.
